title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We present a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single sampled initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) shared across arms + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs were analyzed after preregistered exclusions. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Observed paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair was invoked for 6 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not recorded in the per‑task artifacts and thus could not be evaluated. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We provide preregistered design details, deterministic validator semantics, exact execution accounting and contingency counts, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, contamination findings (no exact public duplicates flagged), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1], [2]. Stochastic LLM generation can produce syntactic and semantic violations—omitted commands, unsafe command orderings, or constraint violations—that pose operational risk when applied to device CLIs. To reduce this risk, research prototypes commonly interpose deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish or header‑space analyses) and bounded automated repair loops in a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture [3], [4].

This study asks a narrowly defined, preregistered estimand: for a fixed single sampled initial candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), does allowing at most one validator‑triggered automated LLM repair increase the proportion of outputs that pass a deterministic network verifier compared to scoring the same initial candidate without repair? The paired design isolates the verifier‑triggered repair effect for identical initial candidates and avoids confounding with independent multi‑sample generation or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies, neither of which were executed under the preregistration. Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation that (a) preserves the registered estimand and shared_initial_candidate semantics, (b) reports exact paired contingency counts and both exact and bootstrap inferential summaries, (c) provides concrete validator traces and representative repaired artifacts, and (d) archives complete execution accounting to support reproducibility.
sections.related_work:
Prior work demonstrates rising interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks and documents common failure modes that motivate grounding and verification [1], [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed in regulated or correctness‑sensitive domains (code generation, formalized workflows) as a mechanism to combine stochastic LLM creativity with deterministic oracles [3]. Network verification tools such as Batfish and header‑space analyses provide deterministic reachability, sequencing, and constraint checks and are natural verifier choices for LLM‑augmented NetOps pipelines; their evolution and verification primitives are documented in prior systems work [4]. Empirical studies focusing on LLM→configuration correctness highlight syntax and sequencing challenges for vendor CLIs, strengthening the case for verifier augmentation [5].

This study differs from prior prototypes and surveys by executing a preregistered paired confirmatory test with archived deterministic validator traces and exact execution manifests. We do not claim general superiority across models or task distributions beyond the specific, preregistered estimand (shared_initial_candidate paired comparison).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered as cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent the same single sampled initial candidate is used to derive the baseline outcome (initial candidate → deterministic validator pass/fail) and the guarded outcome (same candidate → validator; if it fails, at most one automated LLM repair may be invoked; final binary pass/fail recorded). This design isolates the effect of the validator‑triggered repair step on a fixed initial sample.

Task bank and sampling: The preregistered task bank deterministically produced 300 intent→CLI pairs via a deterministic synthetic generator combined with public NetConfEval‑style examples (two vendor dialect clusters: Cisco‑like and Juniper‑like; 150 tasks each). Task generation seeds, generator id, and per‑task manifests are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Inclusion/exclusion, retry, and missingness rules followed the preregistration. Deterministic exclusion logic removed 34 both‑arm provider/model failure episodes (detailed in analysis/missingness_summary.csv), producing 266 complete paired units for the primary analysis.

Model, orchestration, and sampling disclosure: The declared model used for generation and for permitted repair calls was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Archived configuration includes max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset); no deterministic sampling seed was archived. Provider call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34. Stage accounting indicates shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6 (exact counts archived).

Deterministic validator: The binary oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator semantics archived). For each episode the validator performs: CLI syntactic parsing and normalization; required_sequence checks comparing expected_sequence to parsed commands; allowed_touched_fields enforcement; and reachability/constraint validation on the synthetic topology model. Per‑episode validator traces record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, normalized_configuration, and explicit validation_before/validation_after snapshots; these artifacts are available under execution/scoring/*.json and are the source of the binary pass/fail used in analysis.

Repair loop and shared_initial_candidate mechanics: Under the preregistered adapter contract, the same initial sampled candidate was used for both arms (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"). If the validator failed that candidate, the guarded arm could invoke at most one automated LLM repair call; repair prompts included the validator’s failure codes, task constraints, and the request for a corrected configuration. Repair provider traces and any repair prompt SHA‑256 are archived when invoked (repair stage_count = 6 observed).

Analysis plan: The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes at α=0.05 (executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1). Interval estimation used a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the paired difference per preregistration; bootstrap parameters and seed are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Missingness handling used the preregistered complete_pair_primary rule: pairs with both‑arm provider/model failures (34 pairs) were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis; sensitivity analyses treating excluded pairs as failures were also executed.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2); completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68. Complete paired units analyzed = 266; both_missing_pairs = 34 (excluded per preregistration). Model call accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 306 (completed 272, failed 34), cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 272 (deterministic_reconciliation.json). Repair calls recorded = 6 (stage_counts: repair = 6). The reconciliation artifact confirms that cross‑condition cache reuse did not occur and that all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Primary outcomes (complete_pairs = 266): baseline successes = 260; guarded final successes = 265. Paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 260 (both pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed proportions: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015. Paired difference = 0.01879699248. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered α=0.05 decision rule not met). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. The bootstrap CI narrowly excludes zero while the exact McNemar test does not reject at α=0.05; this is consistent with small discordant counts where McNemar’s test is discrete and depends solely on discordant pair counts (here n10=5, n01=0) while the bootstrap CI reflects resampled paired‑difference variability.

Repair behavior and representative artifacts: Repairs were rare (6/300 tasks). Representative example: task‑000008 initial shared candidate (execution/responses/task-000008-shared-initial.txt; sha256 = 89306095ceeedc3df7d752beb035f342edf9e82b7252e45356919e29958245e7) contained an incomplete trailing line "interface uplink2\n" and failed the validator due to parsed_command_count mismatch and missing required sequence. The guarded final artifact (execution/responses/task-000008-guarded.txt; sha256 = d52b7616f93a608409c7ce4eeb21958b8ceeb502faaf302d9b36468d8a627944) contains the corrected full sequence; its validator trace (execution/scoring/task-000008-guarded.json) shows validation_after accepted the normalized_configuration and the episode scored as VALID_CONFIGURATION. All repair prompts, provider traces, and validator before/after snapshots for repaired episodes are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/scoring/ and are available for audit.

Contamination and sensitivity: analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no exact duplicate public tasks; therefore no exact‑public duplicates were excluded from the primary analysis. Sensitivity analysis treating the 34 excluded both‑arm episodes as failures (conservative complete N=300) yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333 but identical discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0) and exact McNemar p = 0.0625, confirming the primary inferential result is robust to the preregistered conservative missingness treatment.

Secondary preregistered estimands: median repair iterations per task = 0 (H2(a) confirmed). Pre‑registered median end‑to‑end latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be evaluated because per‑episode latency was not recorded in the archived task artifacts; this is reported as a preregistered deviation (data missing) and discussed below as a limitation.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The GVR pipeline delivered a small absolute increase in deterministic‑validator pass rate (~1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach statistical significance at α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) excludes zero, illustrating the finite‑sample inferential nuance: McNemar’s exact test depends only on discordant counts and can produce conservative discrete p‑values with few discordants, whereas bootstrap intervals reflect empirical paired‑difference variability. We present both for transparency and to allow practitioner judgement about practical relevance versus formal hypothesis acceptance.

Operational implications: The marginal benefit of a single automated repair was limited because baseline first‑pass acceptance was high (≈97.7%), leaving few opportunities for repair to help. Repair invocations occurred infrequently (6/300), and when they occurred the archived validator traces show they corrected concrete parsing/incompleteness or sequencing defects. For workloads with lower first‑pass accuracy or different error profiles, a bounded repair loop could yield larger ROI. Importantly, under shared_initial_candidate semantics this study does not evaluate designs that rely on multiple independent initial draws, constrained first‑pass prompting, or constrained decoding—those are distinct estimands that should be preregistered and tested separately.

Threats to validity: Internal validity—shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolates validator‑triggered repair for a single sampled candidate; it does not measure benefits obtainable by constrained prompting or by drawing multiple independent candidates. Construct validity—the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a specified finite rule battery (syntactic normalization, required_sequence checks, allowed_touched_fields, reachability on the synthetic topology); semantic errors outside that rule set are unmeasured. External validity—tasks were produced by a deterministic synthetic generator plus public NetConfEval‑style examples limited to two vendor dialect clusters; results may not generalize to other vendors, larger production topologies, or differing workload difficulty distributions. Conclusion validity—discordant counts were low (n10=5, n01=0) and 34 both‑arm provider failures reduced effective N from 300 to 266; these factors reduce precision and the ability to detect small effects.

Design lessons: (1) When baseline pass rates are high, choose tasks with lower baseline accuracy or increase planned N to ensure sufficient discordant counts to power McNemar tests. (2) Record per‑episode latency and pipeline timing in execution artifacts to evaluate operational latency bounds; the preregistered latency estimand could not be assessed here due to missing latency logging. (3) Broaden deterministic verifier rule coverage and instrument verifier false‑negative probes to assess unmeasured semantic failure modes. (4) Consider factorial/preregistered arms that contrast shared_initial_candidate semantics with independent multi‑draw or constrained‑prompting strategies to attribute gains to generation vs repair.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment that measured the effect of a bounded automated repair stage in a GVR pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analyzed pairs the guarded pipeline improved the deterministic validator pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were infrequent (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not recorded and thus the preregistered latency bound could not be evaluated. All execution and analysis artifacts, validator traces, provider call accounting, contingency tables, and reconciliation manifests are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the preregistration to permit audit and reanalysis. Future work should preregister alternative estimands (e.g., multiple independent draws, constrained first‑pass prompting), expand verifier coverage, and ensure per‑episode timing telemetry to evaluate operational bounds.

References
[1] C. Wang, M. Scazzariello, A. Farshin, S. Ferlin, D. Kostić, and M. Chiesa, “NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?,” in Proc. ACM, 2024, doi: 10.1145/3656296.
[2] S. Y. Long, J. Tan, B. Mao, F. Tang, Y. Li, M. Zhao, and N. Kato, “A Survey on Intelligent Network Operations and Performance Optimization Based on Large Language Models,” IEEE Commun. Surveys Tuts., 2025, doi: 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606.
[3] R. Cadenas, “Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments,” SSRN, 2026, doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6754899.
[4] M. Brown, A. Fogel, D. Halperin, V. Heorhiadi, R. Mahajan, and T. Millstein, “Lessons from the evolution of the Batfish configuration analysis tool,” Proc. ACM, 2023, doi: 10.1145/3603269.3604866.
[5] R. Mondal, A. Tang, R. Beckett, T. Millstein, and G. Varghese, “What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?,” Proc. ACM, 2023, doi: 10.1145/3626111.3628194.

Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration: cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Human role and autonomy boundary: before the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the autonomy lock the registered pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, preregistration, experimental execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review simulation, and revision. Nondeterminism disclosure: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) and no deterministic sampling seed is archived; therefore nondeterministic sampling of model outputs cannot be excluded. Execution artifacts, logs, reconciliation manifests, and analysis files referenced in the paper are archived in the evidence bundle linked in the preregistration for audit.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
